# Rubric excerpt — 4.11 Workshop plan

For a checker session that cannot carry all of `EVALUATION-LOOP.md`:
paste this file alongside the checker agent. Item numbers are verbatim,
so citations like "4.11 item 2" resolve here. The loop itself — gate
matrix, iteration cap, escalation, known limits, checkpoints — lives in
the full file and is not restated.

## 2. Verdict schema

Every evaluator ends its report with this block, verbatim in this shape. It is
the machine-readable part — the thing that lets a person, a script, or an
orchestrating agent branch on the result instead of reading prose.

```
=== VERDICT ===
gate:        <agent name>
artifact:    <file or artifact name>
iteration:   <1 | 2 | 3>
result:      PASS | PASS_WITH_FLAGS | FAIL | NOT_APPLICABLE
blocking:    <count>
flags:       <count>
blocking_ids: [<claim/section ids>]
flag_ids:     [<claim/section ids>]
next_action: RELEASE | REVISE | ESCALATE | ROUTE
note:        <one line, plain language>
=== END VERDICT ===
```

**A gate may append gate-specific fields after the standard ones** — as
`research-safety-checker` does with `destination`, `participants`, and
`consent` — provided the standard fields keep their names, order, and meaning,
and the gate's own file documents its extras. Anything that parses the block
reads the standard fields and ignores what follows. What a gate may never do is
redefine or omit a standard field: when an evaluator has to do *that* to be
honest, the block is wrong and this section gets fixed.

### Result semantics

| Result | Meaning | `next_action` |
|---|---|---|
| `PASS` | Nothing blocking, nothing flagged. | `RELEASE` |
| `PASS_WITH_FLAGS` | Nothing blocking. Some items need **human judgment**, not correction. | `RELEASE` |
| `FAIL` | At least one blocking defect. The artifact is wrong, not merely debatable. | `REVISE` (or `ESCALATE` at cap) |
| `NOT_APPLICABLE` | **The artifact is out of this gate's scope and was not reviewed.** Counts are zero because nothing was scored, not because nothing is wrong. `note` must name the gate that owns it. | `ROUTE` |

`NOT_APPLICABLE` is a routing outcome, not a judgment, and it is the only result
that asserts nothing about the artifact. It exists because the other three all
lie in this situation: `PASS` and `PASS_WITH_FLAGS` claim the artifact cleared a
review it never received, and `FAIL` tells the drafter to revise against a rubric
that does not apply to it. A gate handed the wrong artifact type — a survey to
`guide-checker`, a discussion guide to `survey-checker` — returns this, names the
right gate, and stops.

It was added because two gates in separate contexts independently invented the
same value when the schema gave them nothing usable, and one said so in its own
output. When an evaluator has to depart from this block to be honest, the block
is wrong.

Do not use `NOT_APPLICABLE` for an artifact this gate owns but cannot score for
want of an input — that is a `FAIL` or an `ESCALATE`, and §4.7's missing-analysis-
plan case is the worked example.

**Blocking vs. flagged is the most important distinction in this file.**

- **Blocking** = the artifact asserts something untrue, unsupported, or unsafe.
  A hallucinated quote. A statistic the data doesn't support. PII in a
  shareable document. These are defects. They get fixed.
- **Flagged** = the artifact is accurate, but a human should look. An
  unexpected finding outside the study's stated questions. A research question
  no finding addressed. A recommendation with no named owner. These are
  *judgment calls*, and an evaluator that treats them as defects will push the
  researcher to delete interesting things to make a gate go green.

`PASS_WITH_FLAGS` releases. Flags travel with the artifact as a short
**Reviewer Notes** section so the human sees them at the moment of decision,
not in a report they've already closed.

**Plain-language flags are the one exception.** When `research-readability-checker`
flags formal words, academic register, or a long methods section (VOICE item 23),
the producer fixes them before showing the artifact and says in one line what it
changed. Every output the team gets should be simple, clear, and direct, and these
are fixes nobody needs to deliberate over. It uses no revision round and needs no
re-run, unless a change touches a quote, a count, or an attribution, which re-runs
`research-synthesis-checker` as any such edit does (for a workshop plan or
summary, `research-workshop-checker`, which owns how it restates findings). The item stays a flag, not a
block: a gate that hard-fails on style gets switched off.

### 4.11 Workshop plan

Applied by `research-workshop-checker`. A workshop plan is the brief, the agenda
with its activity-to-outcome map, and the facilitation guide where there is one.
Every item here was run blind against `workshop-fixture/` in the testing repo
before the gate existed; the fixture's README records what each run changed.

1. A named decision the workshop serves, with an owner and a date. Or, for a
   workshop that ends in no decision, the named output and who uses it next
2. Outcomes are stated as things that will exist at the end (artifacts,
   decisions, commitments). A state of mind ("alignment," "shared
   understanding") counts only when the plan names the artifact that would
   show it, such as each person's written account of the decision, compared.
   The brief also names what the workshop will not try to do
3. Success is defined in the brief: what is checked at the close, and what is
   checked at a stated later date, by a named person who reports it to the
   decision owner. The later check asks what happened to each decision (held,
   reversed on new evidence, or lapsed), not only how many actions closed
4. The plan says why a workshop beats the lighter option (an async review, a
   decision meeting, 1:1s, or a study). A decision already made is run as a
   readout, not a workshop
5. The workshop type is named, and where types are chained the plan says how
   each one's output feeds the next. More than two in one session is flagged
   as a rule of thumb, not a measured limit; a Design Sprint is one type
6. Attendees are listed by role with their decision rights; the decision owner
   and the people consulted afterwards are named
7. Every agenda block maps to an outcome, and every outcome has a block. Flag
   both directions, as §5 does for findings. Setup, breaks, buffer, and silent
   reading are exempt when the plan marks them as outside the arc
8. Divergent work gives every member a parallel, written channel before open
   discussion: silent individual writing, brainwriting, or individual
   pre-work. An open brainstorm aloud fails it; building on each other once
   that channel has run does not
9. Criteria, weights, and the decision rule are stated before any scoring,
   voting, or deciding, including whether the room's scores are a vote or
   advice to the owner. Votes, scores, and consent signals are committed before
   anyone sees anyone else's (a private ballot, or cards revealed together),
   never a show of hands; and private, not only simultaneous, where the
   decision owner or anyone senior is in the room, because a public reveal
   still shows each vote to them. A structured round of spoken input before
   the owner decides is input, not a vote, and is not held to this; nor are
   the reasons for an objection, which are given aloud after the signal. The
   vote mechanics are stated: votes each, whether they can be stacked, and what
   happens on a tie or near-tie
10. No near-field candidate (the team's own concept, a backlog item, a direct
    competitor's design) and no candidate attributed to an owner is shown
    before the divergent activity it would anchor, unless the plan says why
    exposure is intended, as a Design Sprint's Lightning Demos do. Examples
    can raise the quality of ideas as well as narrow them; the item asks for
    the choice to be made on purpose. In a synthesis workshop the
    researcher's draft themes are an anchor too: partners work from the data
    first
11. Each function's unique knowledge is asked for in its own block or its own
    structured slot, not left to surface in open discussion, and the room is
    told up front who holds which expertise
12. The prompt that opens each activity, and the decide question, are written
    word for word: neutral, one ask each, and presupposing neither the problem
    nor the fix. A follow-up asked only after the first answer ("if not, what
    would change your mind?") is not a second ask. Responsive facilitation
    inside an activity is not held to this
13. Every claim brought in or produced carries an evidence label (`[evidence]`,
    `[team knowledge]` with its source, `[assumption]`, `[decision]`), and the
    plan says outputs will be labeled as they are captured. Candidate
    solutions (a backlog, a prototype, a competitor's design) are not claims:
    they are labeled as candidates, or as `[assumption]` until mapped to
    evidence, which says the same thing. What fails is a candidate with no
    label, or one labeled as evidence. An input that restates a
    finding beyond what the finding says (proxy evidence as direct customer
    behavior, a count dropped or rounded up, a reasoning pattern turned into a
    request) fails this item too, as a flag: the room can check the plan's
    summary against the released findings, which `research-synthesis-checker`
    has already ruled on. **Blocking** where workshop output is
    presented as a research finding, or a dot vote as evidence of user need.
    In a co-design session with customers (`methods/co-design-workshop.md`),
    what participants make and rank is research data, not workshop output:
    the block applies to the team's own output, and to participant output
    presented as prevalence or demand, or not labeled group-generated
14. Timing fits the format: breaks in remote blocks, buffer in the agenda, and
    the decision not left to the final minutes. As rules of thumb: working
    groups of about 5 to 8, or the room split with a shared structure; a
    remote day of about four hours at most; no block past about 90 minutes
    without a break
15. A capture plan names who records what, and decisions and actions are read
    back in the room with owners and dates. An action whose owner is not in the
    room is recorded as proposed until they accept it
16. Participant data shown in the room meets `research-safety-checker`'s
    tables, for each participant type, at each destination: the plan's own
    text at the plan's destination, and what it puts on a board at the
    board's. A board is external while customers can see it; customers
    attending the session do not make the plan external unless they receive
    it. Safety runs once for each destination, and this item follows its
    verdicts rather than holding a version of its own. Recording consent for
    attendees is addressed; any customer or design partner attendance is treated
    as external, with no roadmap commitments. Customers who make, rank, or
    are asked about their own work in a segment make that segment co-design
    research, with a study plan (`methods/co-design-workshop.md`); customers
    who only watch or hear a segment do not. Customers do not attend the
    segments where the team negotiates trade-offs or decides. **Blocking** where those tables
    block at the board's destination (participant names, emails, and phone
    numbers block at every tier), or when participant data reaches anyone the
    study's consent does not cover (consent stricter than the destination
    governs, as it does for `research-safety-checker`)
17. Follow-through is planned: a summary within a stated window, assumptions
    routed to a test, any themes the workshop produces routed to the §9
    checkpoint, and each recommendation citing what it rests on: the findings
    (`depends_on` per `FINDINGS-CONTRACT.md`, or the report's own finding
    numbers when the findings are not records), or its `[team knowledge]` or
    `[assumption]` label when it rests on those. The summary's distribution
    names the people the decision affects who were not in the room
18. Materials go out ahead, and every activity that takes spoken input also
    has a written channel. Attendees are asked for access needs in advance;
    calls are captioned; meaning (votes, categories) is never carried by color
    alone; and the time slot respects stated working hours, not only time
    zones
19. The facilitator holds no stake in the outcome, or the plan handles the
    stake structurally (a co-facilitator for the converge and decide
    segments, an outside facilitator for them, or the evidence presented by
    the facilitator as a participant), not only a declared view. Where the facilitator is junior to
    the decision owner, the facilitator's authority over time and turns is
    agreed with the owner in advance
20. The decision owner attends throughout, or has agreed the criteria and the
    decision rule in advance. An owner who arrives only to decide is deciding
    on a summary of work they did not see
21. The plan states what its evidence covers (which personas, how many
    people, what deployment scale), and where the decision reaches past it,
    that part is labeled `[assumption]` and routed to a test (item 17). Boards
    keep apart the personas the evidence separates (the person who configures
    a product and the daily user, for example).
    The inputs include the findings that cut against the favored option, not
    only the ones for it
22. A dry run with at least one person is scheduled before the day, or the
    agenda has run before unchanged and the last run's evaluation is cited
23. Readability is `research-readability-checker`'s, which runs after this
    gate against `VOICE-AND-STYLE.md`. This item is met when that gate is in
    the plan's sequence; it is not scored here, so one standard is not
    applied twice at two severities
24. Where the decision owner, or anyone senior in the room, owns one of the
    candidates, the plan handles it: that candidate is treated like the others
    (no demo, no "vision" framing ahead of the rest), and its owner speaks
    last and votes privately or simultaneously with everyone else (item 9)
25. The blocks run in an order that works: no block depends on an output that
    a later block produces
26. The plan says how disagreement is handled. In the room, at least one block
    draws out doubt before converging: a premortem, concerns from the
    pre-conversations brought in anonymously, or private positions recorded
    before discussion and compared after. After the room, an objection the
    owner overrules is recorded in the decision log with the owner's response,
    the escalation path and its deadline are named, and the plan says whether
    the decision stands while it is escalated
27. Every function whose knowledge the decision needs, or whose sign-off it
    requires, is in the room, consulted before the day, or consulted afterwards
    by a stated date. A decision with security, compliance, legal, or
    accessibility consequences whose owner is not in the room is recorded as
    "decided pending review," with the reviewer named. Anyone deliberately left
    out of a segment is named, with the reason
28. Seniority and other power gradients are handled structurally, not only
    when a senior person owns a candidate (item 24): anyone senior speaks after
    the others in discussion, and no one senior frames the problem before the
    room has worked on it. Gradients the plan can see (contractors or vendors, a
    lone member of a function, a remote minority, a recently joined team) get a
    structural answer, such as anonymous input for concerns, or everyone on
    their own device when anyone is remote. What leaves the room attributes
    decisions and actions to owners, not opinions or dissent to named people,
    unless they agreed
29. Where partners bring confidential material (vulnerability detail,
    credentials or tokens, a customer's system configuration, contract terms,
    unreleased roadmap), the plan names it and says what reaches the board and
    the summary, judged at their destinations. The whiteboard, any recording,
    and any AI note-taking tool are approved for that material, and attendees
    are told when AI capture is on. **Blocking** when credentials, unremediated
    vulnerability detail, or a customer's system configuration is planned onto
    a board or summary whose destination is wider than the people who need it.
    Who a participant or customer is stays `research-safety-checker`'s (item
    16); this item covers what partners bring
30. Where the decision is hard to reverse (a capability removed, a default or an
    interface changed for existing users, a security posture), the plan says so
    and scales the rigor to it: it names the sign-offs (item 27), brings in the
    findings against the favored option (item 21), and does not rest on an
    unlabeled assumption. A reversible decision names when it will be reviewed
    and what evidence would reverse it
31. Where there is a facilitation guide, each block of more than about 20
    minutes has a cut line, the plan says which block is cut first if time runs
    short (never the decide block or the read-back), and it names the
    facilitator's move for a stall, a two-camp split, and a decision that cannot
    be reached in the room (a deferral with an owner and a date, never a show
    of hands to rescue it)

Items 26 to 31 were appended on 2026-10-13 from the adversarial read's omission
audit, with amendments to items 2, 3, 9, 10, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, and 21. Four of
the six new items are conditional (they apply only where the situation exists),
so a plan is not flagged for omitting what does not concern it.
Items 24 and 25 were appended on 2026-10-13, after independent blind readers
across the fixture's runs raised each with no item to score it against, at
least three readers apiece (for item 25, one was the readability gate). They sit after
item 23 because items are cited by number in `research-workshop-checker` and in
the fixture's key.
Items 19 to 22 were added on 2026-10-13 while building the workshop fixture:
the scenario file taught all four and no item here checked them. Only the
**bold** triggers in items 13, 16, and 29 block. Every other failure of those three
items is a flag, as is every failure of every other item, with one exception.
A plan that names neither a decision nor an output, one whose decision is
already made and that exists to ratify it, and one whose decision rests on
evidence the plan says does not exist yet each count as one blocking item and
escalate (§1): item-level flags on them would be noise, and `FAIL` with
`ESCALATE` needs a blocking item to stand on (§2). Score each defect once,
under the most specific item that names it, and cross-reference the others:
the owner's concept demoed first is item 24, not 10 and 24.

in the testing repo) changed items 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16, 17, 18, 19,
